bibliographic.title: Artificial intelligence for postpartum hemorrhage: a systematic review
bibliographic.authors: AlSaad, R., Yazbek, F., Farrell, T., Albasha, S., Al-Marri, A., & Thomas, R.
bibliographic.citation_apa: AlSaad, R., Yazbek, F., Farrell, T., Albasha, S., Al-Marri, A., & Thomas, R. (2026). Artificial intelligence for postpartum hemorrhage: A systematic review. Frontiers in Global Women's Health, 7, 1806220. https://doi.org/10.3389/fgwh.2026.1806220

methodology.method_family: PRISMA-guided systematic review with modified QUADAS-2 appraisal
methodology.sample_description: 33 studies on AI models for PPH prediction published between 2015 and 2025, screened from MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar
methodology.technology_context: AI predictive models for postpartum hemorrhage risk stratification, early warning, and case identification using classical machine learning, deep learning, and LLM/NLP-based clinical text methods

eligibility.exclusion_reason: Systematic review focused on AI predictive modeling for postpartum hemorrhage; does not address conversational AI, conversational governance, or LLM-based conversational systems.
eligibility.decision_rationale: The article systematically synthesizes clinical prediction models for PPH across classical ML, deep learning, and limited LLM/NLP use (2/33 studies; 6%). It does not examine chatbots, agents, RAG, guardrails, or governance of conversational LLM deployments. Brief mentions of post-deployment monitoring and governance relate to predictive model recalibration, not conversational governance in regulated LLM systems.

appraisal.notes: As a standalone systematic review on PPH prediction, methods appear sound (PRISMA, dual screening, modified QUADAS-2, prespecified extraction). Transferability to conversational LLM governance is low because the topic, outcomes, and technology focus differ substantially from the review scope.

cerqual.explanation: The review is internally coherent and methodologically adequate for synthesizing PPH prediction evidence, but its relevance to conversational governance of LLM systems in regulated environments is very low; LLM and governance content are peripheral.

coding.theme: AI-based clinical prediction for obstetric hemorrhage risk
coding.subtheme: Emerging but minor role of LLM/NLP in clinical documentation-based PPH prediction

synthesis.main_claim: AI-based PPH prediction research is expanding rapidly but remains constrained by retrospective closed datasets, heterogeneous outcomes, limited external validation, and predominance of classical ML over deep learning and LLM approaches.
synthesis.contribution: Provides a PRISMA-guided synthesis of 33 studies on AI for PPH prediction, characterizing model families, validation practices, and quality concerns; notes LLM-based approaches in only 6% of included studies and briefly recommends post-deployment governance for recalibration and drift detection.
synthesis.limitations: Included evidence is largely retrospective, single-site, and internally validated; participant selection bias is common; LLM and conversational applications are minimally represented.
synthesis.use_in_review: Exclude from central evidence on conversational LLM governance; at most marginal contextual reference for healthcare AI deployment monitoring and the limited use of LLM/NLP in regulated clinical prediction settings.

evidence.claim: Article is a systematic review on AI for PPH prediction, not conversational LLM governance.
evidence.excerpt: To systematically synthesize the evidence on AI models for PPH prediction, including clinical applications, data sources, prediction targets, validation strategies, and study quality.

evidence.claim: LLM-based approaches are a minor subset of included studies.
No conversational AI focus is present in the provided text.
evidence.excerpt: Classical machine learning dominated (85%), while deep learning (33%) and LLM-based approaches (6%) were less frequent.

evidence.claim: LLM/NLP is positioned for clinical text extraction in prediction, not conversational systems.
evidence.excerpt: LLM/NLP-based approaches were positioned as emerging methods for extracting or modeling risk-relevant information from clinical text.

evidence.claim: Governance mention relates to predictive model post-deployment monitoring, not conversational governance.
evidence.excerpt: Post-deployment monitoring should be pre-specified, with governance for recalibration, drift detection, and model updating over time.

evidence.claim: Review used rigorous systematic review methods.
evidence.excerpt: We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review of studies published between 2015 and 2025 across MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar.

evidence.claim: Dual independent screening and consensus resolution were used.
evidence.excerpt: Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data using a prespecified form, and resolved disagreements by consensus.

evidence.claim: Quality appraisal used modified QUADAS-2 tailored to AI-based PPH prediction.
evidence.excerpt: Risk of bias and applicability were appraised using a modified QUADAS-2 tool tailored to AI-based PPH prediction.

evidence.claim: Main quality concern in included primary studies was participant selection bias.
evidence.excerpt: Participant selection was the main quality concern (high risk of bias: 48%)

evidence.claim: Validation in included studies was predominantly internal with limited external validation.
evidence.excerpt: Validation was mainly internal (76%), with limited external validation.

evidence.claim: Study is set in regulated healthcare domain.
evidence.excerpt: Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) remains a leading cause of maternal morbidity and mortality

evidence.claim: Generative AI was used only for manuscript preparation, not as study subject.
evidence.excerpt: During the preparation of this manuscript, artificial intelligence tools were used to assist with English language refinement and formatting of Figures 2–5.
